title: Random Walks and Markov Chains

intro.x: Many random systems evolve step by step, with the next step depending only on the present state. This chapter starts with the simplest example, the random walk, and solves the gambler’s ruin problem completely. It then develops the general theory of Markov chains: transition matrices, classification of states, hitting times, stationary distributions, and convergence to equilibrium.

blocks.x: Let $X_1,X_2,\dots$ be independent with $\Prob(X_i=+1)=p$ and $\Prob(X_i=-1)=q=1-p$. The simple random walk started at $S_0=k$ is $S_n=k+X_1+\dots+X_n$. It moves up or down one unit per step. For $p=\tfrac12$ the walk is symmetric.
Gambler’s ruin

A gambler starts with $k$ units ($0\le k\le N$) and bets one unit per round, winning with probability $p$. Play stops at $0$ (ruin) or $N$ (target). Let $h_k$ be the probability of reaching $N$ before $0$.
With $r=q/p$,
h_k=\begin{cases}\dfrac kN,&p=\tfrac12,\\[1em]\dfrac{1-r^k}{1-r^N},&p\ne\tfrac12.\end{cases}
Conditioning on the first step (law of total probability) gives, for $1\le k\le N-1$,

Writing $1=p+q$ and rearranging, $p(h_{k+1}-h_k)=q(h_k-h_{k-1})$, so with $d_k=h_k-h_{k-1}$ we have $d_{k+1}=r\,d_k$ and hence $d_k=r^{k-1}d_1$. Summing the differences, $h_k=\sum_{j=1}^kd_j=d_1\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}r^j$. If $r=1$ this is $kd_1$, and $h_N=1$ gives $d_1=1/N$. If $r\ne1$ it is $d_1(1-r^k)/(1-r)$, and $h_N=1$ gives $d_1=(1-r)/(1-r^N)$.

A gambler with $\$90$ aims for $\$100$ in a fair game, one dollar per bet: $h_{90}=0.9$. In a casino roulette game with $p=18/38$ ($r=10/9$) the probability of success is $\dfrac{1-(10/9)^{90}}{1-(10/9)^{100}}\approx(9/10)^{10}\approx0.35$, far smaller, although the game is only mildly unfavourable: the long run of bets amplifies the small negative drift.

blocks.name: Corollary
blocks.title: Ruin with an infinitely rich opponent

blocks.x: Starting at $k\ge1$, the probability that the walk ever reaches $0$ is $(q/p)^k$ if $p>\tfrac12$, and $1$ if $p\le\tfrac12$.

The walk reaches $0$ before $N$ with probability $1-h_k$. As $N\to\infty$ the events “reach $0$ before $N$” increase to “ever reach $0$”, so by continuity of probability the limit of $1-h_k$ is the answer. For $p>\tfrac12$, $r<1$ and $1-h_k\to1-(1-r^k)=r^k$. For $p<\tfrac12$, $r>1$ and $1-h_k=\frac{r^N-r^k}{r^N-1}\to1$. For $p=\tfrac12$, $1-h_k=1-k/N\to1$.
Let $D_k$ be the expected number of rounds until play stops. Then

D_k=k(N-k)\ \ (p=\tfrac12),\qquad
D_k=\frac k{q-p}-\frac N{q-p}\cdot\frac{1-r^k}{1-r^N}\ \ (p\ne\tfrac12).

First-step analysis gives $D_k=1+pD_{k+1}+qD_{k-1}$ with $D_0=D_N=0$ (finiteness of $D_k$ is shown in Chapter 14). For $p=\tfrac12$ try $D_k=k(N-k)$: $1+\frac12(k+1)(N-k-1)+\frac12(k-1)(N-k+1)=1+k(N-k)-1=k(N-k)$. The solution of the recurrence with the boundary conditions is unique (the difference of two solutions satisfies the homogeneous equation with zero boundary values, hence is $0$ by the maximum principle), so this is it. For $p\ne\tfrac12$, a particular solution is $k/(q-p)$ (check: $1+\frac{p(k+1)+q(k-1)}{q-p}=1+\frac{k-(q-p)}{q-p}=\frac k{q-p}$), and the homogeneous solutions are $A+Br^k$. The boundary conditions give $D_k=\frac k{q-p}-\frac N{q-p}\cdot\frac{1-r^k}{1-r^N}$.
For the fair game, $D_k=k(N-k)$: a fair game between a gambler with $1$ unit and a casino with $N-1$ units lasts on average $N-1$ rounds, yet the gambler is ruined with probability $1-1/N$.
Reflection principle and the maximum
Visualise the walk as a path $(0,S_0),(1,S_1),\dots,(n,S_n)$ in the plane.
Let $x,y>0$. The number of paths from $(0,x)$ to $(n,y)$ that touch or cross the level $0$ equals the number of paths from $(0,-x)$ to $(n,y)$.

Given a path from $(0,x)$ to $(n,y)$ that touches $0$, let $t$ be the first time it does so, and reflect the portion before $t$ in the horizontal axis (replace $S_j$ by $-S_j$ for $j\le t$). This yields a path from $(0,-x)$ that reaches $0$ at time $t$ and then continues to $(n,y)$. The map is a bijection onto paths from $(0,-x)$ to $(n,y)$, since any such path must cross $0$ (it starts below and ends above), and reflecting its initial segment up to the first touch gives the inverse.
For the symmetric simple random walk from $0$ and an integer $a\ge1$,

\Prob\Bigl(\max_{0\le k\le n}S_k\ge a\Bigr)=\Prob(S_n\ge a)+\Prob(S_n>a)
=2\,\Prob(S_n>a)+\Prob(S_n=a).

Split according to the final value. If $S_n\ge a$ the maximum is at least $a$ (the path ends above or at $a$). If $S_n=b<a$ and the maximum is at least $a$, the path touches the level $a$; by the reflection principle (reflecting across $a$, shifting the origin) the number of such paths equals the number of paths ending at $2a-b>a$. Since all paths have probability $2^{-n}$, $\Prob(\max\ge a,S_n=b)=\Prob(S_n=2a-b)$ for $b<a$. Summing over $b<a$ gives $\Prob(S_n>a)$. Adding $\Prob(S_n\ge a)$ gives the claim.
For the symmetric walk, $\Prob(S_{2n}=0)=\binom{2n}n4^{-n}\sim1/\sqrt{\pi n}$, and the walk returns to $0$ with probability $1$ (recurrence).

The first claim: among the $2^{2n}$ paths, those with $n$ ups and $n$ downs number $\binom{2n}n$; the asymptotics follow from Stirling’s formula $n!\sim\sqrt{2\pi n}(n/e)^n$ (cited). For recurrence let $u_{2n}=\Prob(S_{2n}=0)$ and let $f_{2m}$ be the probability that the first return is at time $2m$. Decomposing on the time of the first return, $u_{2n}=\sum_{m=1}^nf_{2m}u_{2n-2m}$ for $n\ge1$, with $u_0=1$. In generating functions $U(s)=\sum_{n\ge0}u_{2n}s^{2n}$ and $F(s)=\sum_{m\ge1}f_{2m}s^{2m}$ this reads $U=1+FU$, i.e. $F=1-1/U$. By the binomial series, $\binom{2n}n4^{-n}=(-1)^n\binom{-1/2}n$, so $U(s)=(1-s^2)^{-1/2}$ for $\abs s<1$. Hence $F(s)=1-\sqrt{1-s^2}\to1$ as $s\uparrow1$, i.e. $\sum_mf_{2m}=1$: the walk returns with probability $1$.

blocks.name: Nuance
blocks.title: recurrent but with infinite expected return time

blocks.x: $F(s)=1-\sqrt{1-s^2}$ has an infinite derivative at $s=1$, so the expected time to return to $0$ is $\infty$. The symmetric walk returns for sure, but typically after a very long time ($\Prob(\text{first return}>2n)=\Prob(S_{2n}=0)\sim1/\sqrt{\pi n}$, which is not summable). Such a state is called null recurrent.
A sequence $X_0,X_1,\dots$ of random variables taking values in a finite or countable state space $\mathcal S$ is a (time-homogeneous) Markov chain if for all $n$ and all states,
\Prob(X_{n+1}=j\given X_n=i,X_{n-1}=i_{n-1},\dots,X_0=i_0)=\Prob(X_{n+1}=j\given X_n=i)=p_{ij}.
The matrix $P=(p_{ij})$ is the transition matrix: $p_{ij}\ge0$ and $\sum_jp_{ij}=1$ for every $i$.
The defining property, the Markov property, says that given the present state, the past is irrelevant to the future.
With initial distribution $\mu_i=\Prob(X_0=i)$,
\Prob(X_0=i_0,X_1=i_1,\dots,X_n=i_n)=\mu_{i_0}p_{i_0i_1}\cdots p_{i_{n-1}i_n}.

Consequently the $n$-step transition probabilities $p_{ij}^{(n)}=\Prob(X_n=j\given X_0=i)$ are the entries of the matrix power $P^n$, and $p^{(m+n)}_{ij}=\sum_kp^{(m)}_{ik}p^{(n)}_{kj}$. The law of $X_n$ is the row vector $\mu P^n$.

The product formula follows from the chain rule (Theorem 3.3) and the Markov property. Summing it over $i_1,\dots,i_{n-1}$ gives $p_{ij}^{(n)}$ as the $(i,j)$ entry of the product of $n$ copies of $P$ (matrix multiplication is exactly this sum). The identity $P^{m+n}=P^mP^n$ is the Chapman–Kolmogorov equation. The last claim is total probability: $\Prob(X_n=j)=\sum_i\mu_ip^{(n)}_{ij}$.
States $\{1,2\}$, $P=\begin{pmatrix}1-a&a\\b&1-b\end{pmatrix}$ with $a,b\in(0,1)$. Solving $p^{(n+1)}_{11}=p^{(n)}_{11}(1-a)+p^{(n)}_{12}b=p^{(n)}_{11}(1-a-b)+b$ gives
p^{(n)}_{11}=\frac b{a+b}+\frac a{a+b}(1-a-b)^n,
which tends to $b/(a+b)$ geometrically fast. The vector $\pi=(\frac b{a+b},\frac a{a+b})$ satisfies $\pi P=\pi$.
Random walk on a graph: from vertex $i$ move to a uniformly chosen neighbour: $p_{ij}=1/\deg(i)$ if $i\sim j$.
Gambler’s ruin chain: states $0,\dots,N$; $0$ and $N$ absorbing.
Ehrenfest urn: $N$ balls in two urns; each step a uniformly random ball is moved to the other urn; the state is the number of balls in urn 1.
Card shuffling: the state is a permutation of the deck; each shuffle applies a random permutation.
Classification of states

State $j$ is accessible from $i$ ($i\to j$) if $p^{(n)}_{ij}>0$ for some $n\ge0$; $i$ and $j$ communicate ($i\leftrightarrow j$) if each is accessible from the other. Communication is an equivalence relation; its classes are the communicating classes. The chain is irreducible if there is one class. The period of $i$ is $\gcd\{n\ge1:p^{(n)}_{ii}>0\}$; $i$ is aperiodic if the period is $1$. (Period is constant on a class.)
Let $T_i=\min\{n\ge1:X_n=i\}$ be the first return time to $i$, and $f_i=\Prob_i(T_i<\infty)$ (subscript $i$: the chain starts at $i$).
State $i$ is recurrent if $f_i=1$ and transient if $f_i<1$. A recurrent state is positive recurrent if $\Exp_i[T_i]<\infty$ and null recurrent otherwise.
Let $V_i$ be the total number of visits to $i$ (counting time $0$) when starting at $i$. Then $V_i$ is geometric: $\Prob_i(V_i=m)=f_i^{m-1}(1-f_i)$. Hence
i\text{ is recurrent}\iff\Prob_i(V_i=\infty)=1\iff\sum_{n=0}^\infty p^{(n)}_{ii}=\infty,
and $i$ is transient iff $\sum_np^{(n)}_{ii}<\infty$.

By the Markov property, each time the chain is at $i$ it returns with probability $f_i$, independently of the past. So $\Prob_i(V_i\ge m)=f_i^{m-1}$. If $f_i<1$ then $V_i$ is a.s. finite with mean $\Exp_i[V_i]=1/(1-f_i)<\infty$; if $f_i=1$ then $V_i=\infty$ a.s. Finally $\Exp_i[V_i]=\sum_n\Exp_i[\indic_{\{X_n=i\}}]=\sum_np^{(n)}_{ii}$.

Recurrence is a class property: if $i\leftrightarrow j$ and $i$ is recurrent, so is $j$. In a finite chain every recurrent class is positive recurrent, and every state in a class that is not closed (can be left) is transient. A finite irreducible chain is positive recurrent.

Choose $r,s$ with $p^{(r)}_{ij}>0$, $p^{(s)}_{ji}>0$. Then $p^{(r+n+s)}_{jj}\ge p^{(s)}_{ji}p^{(n)}_{ii}p^{(r)}_{ij}$, and summing over $n$ shows $\sum_np^{(n)}_{jj}=\infty$. (The other assertions follow from the criterion and the geometric trials argument; see the exercises.)

The symmetric simple random walk on $\Z^d$ is recurrent for $d=1,2$ and transient for $d\ge3$ (P'olya). For $d=1$ we showed this directly. For $d=3$, $\Prob(S_{2n}=0)\asymp n^{-3/2}$, which is summable, so by Theorem 12.14 the origin is transient. In the memorable phrase, “a drunk man will find his way home, but a drunk bird may get lost forever”.
Hitting probabilities and times
Let $A\subseteq\mathcal S$ and define $h_i=\Prob_i(\text{chain ever hits }A)$ and $k_i=\Exp_i[\text{time to hit }A]$.

The vector $h$ satisfies $h_i=1$ for $i\in A$ and $h_i=\sum_jp_{ij}h_j$ for $i\notin A$; it is the minimal non-negative solution of these equations. The vector $k$ is the minimal non-negative solution of $k_i=0$ for $i\in A$, $k_i=1+\sum_jp_{ij}k_j$ for $i\notin A$.

That $h$ solves the equations is first-step analysis. For minimality, let $x$ be any non-negative solution and let $h_i^{(n)}=\Prob_i(\text{hit }A\text{ within }n\text{ steps})$. Then $h^{(0)}_i=\indic_{A}(i)\le x_i$, and if $h^{(n)}\le x$ then $h^{(n+1)}_i=\sum_jp_{ij}h^{(n)}_j\le\sum_jp_{ij}x_j=x_i$ for $i\notin A$. So $h^{(n)}\le x$ for all $n$, and $h^{(n)}\uparrow h$. The argument for $k$ is the same.

blocks.name: Nuance
blocks.title: minimality matters on infinite state spaces

blocks.x: For gambler’s ruin on $\{0,1,2,\dots\}$ with $p>\tfrac12$, both $h_k\equiv1$ and $h_k=(q/p)^k$ solve the equations for hitting $0$, but the true probability is the smaller one. In finite chains where $A$ is reached with probability $1$ from every state, the solution is unique.

Suppose the states are split into transient states $\mathcal T$ and absorbing states $\mathcal A$, with $P=\begin{pmatrix}Q&R\\0&I\end{pmatrix}$ ($Q$ for transitions among transient states, $R$ for transient$\to$absorbing). Then $I-Q$ is invertible, the matrix $N=(I-Q)^{-1}=\sum_{n\ge0}Q^n$ has entries $N_{ij}=\Exp_i[\text{visits to }j]$, the expected time to absorption from $i$ is $\sum_jN_{ij}$, and the absorption probabilities are $B=NR$.

$Q^n_{ij}=\Prob_i(X_n=j)$ for transient $j$, so $\sum_nQ^n_{ij}$ is the expected number of visits to $j$. Absorption occurs eventually with probability one (finite chain, every transient state leads to absorption), so $Q^n\to0$, which implies the Neumann series $\sum Q^n$ converges and equals $(I-Q)^{-1}$ (multiply $(I-Q)\sum_{m\le n}Q^m=I-Q^{n+1}$ and let $n\to\infty$). The probability of absorbing at $a$ from $i$ is $\sum_n\sum_jQ^n_{ij}R_{ja}=(NR)_{ia}$, summing over the time of the last transient step.
A probability vector $\pi$ (row, non-negative, $\sum\pi_i=1$) is stationary (or invariant) if $\pi P=\pi$. If $X_0\sim\pi$ then $X_n\sim\pi$ for all $n$.

Let the chain be irreducible and recurrent, fix a state $i$, and define $\gamma_j=\Exp_i\Bigl[\sum_{n=0}^{T_i-1}\indic_{\{X_n=j\}}\Bigr]$, the expected number of visits to $j$ in one excursion from $i$. Then $\gamma P=\gamma$, $\gamma_i=1$, and $\sum_j\gamma_j=\Exp_i[T_i]$. Consequently, if the chain is positive recurrent, $\pi_j=\gamma_j/\Exp_i[T_i]$ is a stationary distribution and in particular $\pi_i=1/\Exp_i[T_i]$.
Write $\gamma_j=\sum_{n\ge0}\Prob_i(X_n=j,T_i>n)$. Then
(\gamma P)_k=\sum_{n\ge0}\sum_j\Prob_i(X_n=j,T_i>n)p_{jk}=\sum_{n\ge0}\Prob_i(X_{n+1}=k,T_i>n),

by the Markov property (the event $\{T_i>n\}$ depends on $X_0,\dots,X_n$ only). If $k\ne i$, then on $\{X_{n+1}=k\}$ we have $T_i>n\iff T_i>n+1$, so $(\gamma P)_k=\sum_{n\ge0}\Prob_i(X_{n+1}=k,T_i>n+1)=\sum_{m\ge1}\Prob_i(X_m=k,T_i>m)=\gamma_k$ (the term $m=0$ is $0$ since $X_0=i\ne k$). If $k=i$, $(\gamma P)_i=\sum_{n\ge0}\Prob_i(X_{n+1}=i,T_i>n)=\sum_{n\ge0}\Prob_i(T_i=n+1)=1=\gamma_i$, using recurrence. Finally $\sum_j\gamma_j=\Exp_i\sum_{n<T_i}1=\Exp_i[T_i]$.
Let the chain be finite, irreducible and aperiodic. Then it has a unique stationary distribution $\pi$, all $\pi_j>0$, and for some $C<\infty$ and $\rho\in(0,1)$,
\max_{i}\sum_j\bigl\lvert p^{(n)}_{ij}-\pi_j\bigr\rvert\le C\rho^n\qquad\text{for all }n.

Positivity of a power. For a finite, irreducible, aperiodic chain there is $m$ such that $p^{(m)}_{ij}>0$ for all $i,j$. (Aperiodicity makes the set of return times to $i$ closed under addition with gcd $1$, hence containing all large integers, a standard number-theoretic fact; irreducibility then connects different states.) Let $\epsilon=\min_{i,j}p^{(m)}_{ij}>0$. A stationary $\pi$ exists by Theorem 12.20 (a finite irreducible chain is positive recurrent).

Coupling. Let $(X_n)$ start at $i$ and $(Y_n)$ start from $\pi$, independent, both with transition matrix $P$. Let $\tau=\min\{n:X_n=Y_n\}$. In each block of $m$ steps, whatever the states $x,y$ at the start of the block, $\Prob(X_{(k+1)m}=Y_{(k+1)m}\given\text{past}) \ge\sum_jp^{(m)}_{xj}p^{(m)}_{yj}\ge\epsilon\sum_jp^{(m)}_{xj}=\epsilon$. Hence $\Prob(\tau>km)\le(1-\epsilon)^k$. Define $\tilde X_n=X_n$ for $n<\tau$ and $\tilde X_n=Y_n$ for $n\ge\tau$; by the strong Markov property $(\tilde X_n)$ is also a Markov chain with matrix $P$ started at $i$ (we use this without detailed proof). Since $Y_n\sim\pi$ and $\tilde X_n$ has the same law as $X_n$,

\bigl\lvert p^{(n)}_{ij}-\pi_j\bigr\rvert=\bigl\lvert\Prob(\tilde X_n=j)-\Prob(Y_n=j)\bigr\rvert
\le\Prob(\tilde X_n=j,Y_n\ne j)+\Prob(Y_n=j,\tilde X_n\ne j).

Summing over $j$, each outcome with $\tilde X_n\ne Y_n$ is counted at most twice, and $\{\tilde X_n\ne Y_n\}=\{\tau>n\}$, so $\sum_j\abs{p^{(n)}_{ij}-\pi_j}\le2\Prob(\tau>n)\le2(1-\epsilon)^{\lfloor n/m\rfloor}$. This gives the bound with $\rho=(1-\epsilon)^{1/m}$. The same argument applied to a second stationary $\pi'$ shows $\pi'=\pi$ (it is stationary, so the distribution stays $\pi'$ while converging to $\pi$). Positivity of $\pi$: $\pi_j=\sum_i\pi_ip^{(m)}_{ij}\ge\epsilon>0$.

blocks.name: Nuance
blocks.title: aperiodicity is needed for convergence of $P^n$, not for existence of $\pi$

blocks.x: Take $P=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ (period $2$). Then $\pi=(\frac12,\frac12)$ is stationary, but $P^n$ alternates between $P$ and $I$ and does not converge. For periodic chains one has convergence of time averages (the ergodic theorem: the fraction of time spent in state $j$ tends to $\pi_j$ almost surely, cited) but not of the distribution.
If a probability vector $\pi$ satisfies $\pi_ip_{ij}=\pi_jp_{ji}$ for all $i,j$, then $\pi$ is stationary.
$(\pi P)_j=\sum_i\pi_ip_{ij}=\sum_i\pi_jp_{ji}=\pi_j\sum_ip_{ji}=\pi_j$.

For the walk on a finite connected graph, take $\pi_i=\deg(i)/(2\abs E)$. Detailed balance holds: for adjacent $i,j$, $\pi_ip_{ij}=\frac{\deg i}{2\abs E}\cdot\frac1{\deg i} =\frac1{2\abs E}=\pi_jp_{ji}$. So the stationary probability is proportional to degree; and $\Exp_i[T_i]=2\abs E/\deg(i)$.

With $N$ balls, the stationary distribution is $\mathrm{Bin}(N,\tfrac12)$: check detailed balance with $\pi_k=\binom Nk2^{-N}$ and $p_{k,k+1}=(N-k)/N$, $p_{k+1,k}=(k+1)/N$: $\binom Nk\frac{N-k}N=\binom N{k+1}\frac{k+1}N$ (both equal $\frac{N!}{k!(N-k-1)!\,N}$).

blocks.name: Interview check
blocks.title: what to do with a Markov chain problem

blocks.x: (1) Define the state space so that the future depends only on the state. (2) For expected times or probabilities of events, solve the first-step equations (Theorem 12.17). (3) For long-run behaviour, solve $\pi P=\pi$, trying detailed balance first. (4) For absorbing problems, compute $N=(I-Q)^{-1}$. Typical interview examples: expected time to see a pattern, expected rolls to see all faces, random walk on a cube, “drunkard on a circle”.
A random walk on $\{0,1,2,3,4\}$ with absorbing ends $0,4$ and fair steps. Find the absorption probabilities and expected duration from each state, using Theorem 12.18.
For the symmetric walk, show the probability that it never returns to $0$ in the first $2n$ steps is $\Prob(S_{2n}=0)$.

A rat walks on the corners of a cube, moving to a uniformly random adjacent corner each step. Find the expected time to return to the starting corner, and the expected time to reach the opposite corner.
Show that for a finite irreducible chain $\Exp_j[T_i]<\infty$ for all $i,j$ (hint: from every state $i$ reachable within $m$ steps with probability $\ge\epsilon$; geometric trials).
Prove that in a finite chain every closed communicating class is positive recurrent, and every communicating class that is not closed consists of transient states.
Draw the transition graph and find the stationary distribution of the chain on $\{1,2,3\}$ with $P=\begin{pmatrix}\frac12&\frac12&0\\ \frac13&\frac13&\frac13\\0&\frac12&\frac12\end{pmatrix}$.
Show that if $\pi$ is stationary for an irreducible chain then $\pi_i>0$ for all $i$.
Show that a time-reversed stationary Markov chain, $Y_n=X_{N-n}$, is Markov with $\hat p_{ij}=\pi_jp_{ji}/\pi_i$, and that the chain is reversible iff $\hat P=P$.
(Challenge) Derive the expected number of rolls of a fair die to see all six faces via the Markov chain on the number of faces seen, and compare with the coupon collector answer $6H_6=14.7$.
